description: We are a creative team participating in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, working on Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map. Our mission is to turn Mars data into an interactive map that helps future explorers understand the Martian environment, identify resources, and navigate potential hazards. We welcome coders, designers, data analysts, and space enthusiasts ready to turn bold ideas into reality. Let's map the future of Mars.
summary:
REDLINE is an interactive Mars exploration and surface-traverse planning workspace developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge (“Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map”). It bridges planetary data silos by integrating an interactive 3D geographic globe, regional mapping, and multi-mission layers—including Viking color mosaics, global and controlled CTX imagery, MGS MOLA shaded relief, HiRISE footprints, and 15 verified planetary reference points.

To address the challenge, REDLINE transitions Mars cartography from static visualization into an evidence-first mission-planning tool. Rather than confusing 2D imagery with elevation, it couples native numerical terrain data with deterministic A* pathfinding. Users can evaluate hypothetical surface traverses across a 10,609-cell native HRSC Digital Elevation Model (DEM), balancing shortest distance against terrain costs derived from directional slope, roughness, and configurable vehicle profiles, alongside provisional travel-time estimation.

REDLINE is vital because interplanetary survival demands scientific transparency. By strictly separating visual maps from numerical elevation, acknowledging coverage limits, and communicating data uncertainty rather than masking it, REDLINE equips future explorers and planners with defensible, reproducible decision support.
details:
Project Details: REDLINE

1. What does it do or how does it work?

REDLINE is an evidence-first Mars mission-intelligence and surface-traverse planning workspace. It transforms planetary cartography from passive visual browsing into an active, deterministic decision-support tool for future human and robotic exploration.

The application functions across three integrated layers:

  • Dual-Scale Spatial Navigation: Users begin at a global scale on an interactive 3D geographic Mars globe powered by Three.js. As they zoom in or select a target of interest (such as Jezero Crater), the interface transitions into a high-precision regional OpenLayers cartographic canvas, preserving orientation and camera angles.
    • Path A (Shortest Distance): The direct geometric baseline through passable terrain.
    • Path B (Terrain-Optimal): Minimizes accumulated slope penalties, directional uphill climb grades, downhill descent limits, and surface roughness.
  • Provisional Travel-Time (ETA): The system computes segment-by-segment duration using actual ground distance, directional slope resistance, configurable speed profiles (Survey, Transit, Custom), and mission operational holds, exporting complete JSON telemetry reports.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Eliminates the "Visual Elevation" Fallacy: Traditional web maps display 2D RGB orbital photos that look deceptively flat. REDLINE separates visual imagery from numerical elevation data, preventing users from routing into invisible 18° cliffs, deep sand traps, or hazardous boulder fields.
  • Transparent Trade-Off Analysis: Rather than presenting a single "magic" path, REDLINE presents the trade-offs side by side: saving 150 meters of distance may demand an unsustainable slope climb that risks vehicle rollover or battery exhaustion.
  • Unified Planetary Context: Combines 40 years of disparate orbital observations into one synchronized viewport, eliminating the need to cross-reference multiple disconnected databases.
  • Client-Side Accessibility & Speed: Performs sub-second graph pathfinding and terrain analysis directly in the browser with zero cloud computing dependencies or backend latency.
  • Responsive Across Form Factors: Operates seamlessly across ultra-wide monitors, laptops, tablets, and mobile devices (down to 320 px) with native touch controls and map-picking workflows.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Operational Mission Planning: Provides planetary scientists, mission planners, and future astronaut support teams with an open, transparent sandbox to model hypothetical surface traverses and assess mechanical, energy, and timing costs.
  • Planetary Science Education: Demystifies complex orbital data for students, educators, and the public, teaching the practical realities of Martian topography, geomorphology, and robotic mobility.
  • Blueprint for Interplanetary Survival Tools: Serves as a prototype for heads-up display (HUD) systems on future astronaut Extravehicular Activity (EVA) spacesuits and autonomous rover pathfinding architectures, demonstrating how multi-source orbital data can guide boots on the ground.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages & Frameworks: TypeScript (~5.9), React 19, HTML5, Tailwind CSS v4.
  • Mapping & 3D Rendering: OpenLayers 10 (regional coordinate mapping, raster tile pipelines), Three.js (interactive 3D geographic Mars globe and visual orientation models).
  • Algorithms & Mathematics: Custom deterministic A* pathfinding engine with non-square spherical geodesy, cross-verified against an independent Dijkstra solver.
  • Scientific Audit & Data Preparation: Python (spiceypy for SPICE orbital kernels, rasterio for GeoTIFF parsing, numpy, python-pptx), Node.js data processing pipelines.
  • Testing & Quality Assurance: Vitest (825 unit and integration tests across 59 test suites), Playwright/Chromium (19 automated browser acceptance test suites), ESLint.
  • Hardware Requirements: Developed and deployed on standard commercial workstations running Windows 11 and PowerShell; builds into standard static web assets runnable on any modern web browser or lightweight host.

5. How is your project creative?

  • “Uncertainty by Design”: Most map applications conceal missing data or interpolate false numbers to look finished. REDLINE embraces scientific honesty: when data coverage ends or vertical height datums exhibit unresolved offsets (such as the −68 m to +29 m offset between CTX and HRSC), REDLINE prominently displays a “Scientific Validation: Partial” badge with clickable, audit-grade receipts and source citations.
  • Dual-Path Comparative Storytelling: Placing the geometric shortest path directly against the terrain-optimal path visually educates the user on why Martian rovers rarely travel in straight lines.
  • Dynamic Vehicle Kinematics in Real Time: Allows users to adjust rover slope thresholds and speed sensitivities on the fly and immediately watch the path and ETA timeline recalculate without reloading data.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Non-Negotiable Scientific Integrity: We strictly adhered to the rule of never fabricating NASA/ESA observations, coordinates, hazard ratings, or safety probabilities.
  • Martian Coordinate Reference Systems: We respected planetary datums (planetocentric vs. planetographic latitudes, 3,396,000 m reference spheres) and verified coordinate transformations against independent PROJ baselines rather than assuming terrestrial Web Mercator conventions.
  • Kinematic Asymmetry: Climbing uphill consumes vastly more power and traction than level transit, while steep descents risk uncontrolled slides; our model penalizes uphill and downhill grades asymmetrically and prevents diagonal corner-cutting across forbidden cells.
  • Operational Reality: Real planetary surface traverses include mandatory scientific sampling stops, communication windows, and battery recharges; REDLINE explicitly isolates operational holds from movement durations.
  • Accessibility & Performance: Ensured strict keyboard navigation, visible focus indicators, readable contrast across dark mission-control palettes, and lightweight tile caching to avoid bandwidth bottlenecks.
